sentences.text: Drinking-water quality guidelines identify microbiological, physical, chemical and radiological parameters that have been found in drinking water.
Health Canada has established more than 100 objectives for a host of contaminants in drinking water.

Guidelines recommend measuring concentrations of chemical substances such as metals (e.g., lead, mercury) and other inorganic compounds, pesticides, radionuclides, and drinking water disinfection by-products (e.g., trihalomethanes) as well as microbial parameters such as bacteria, viruses and parasites in raw, treated and distributed drinking water.
Densities of disease-causing organisms or concentrations of hazardous or toxic chemicals or radioactive substances should not exceed human health objectives, standards, or guidelines.
Most contaminants in drinking water rarely exceed guidelines and many are below their analytical detection limit.
Guidelines are based on lifetime exposures and have been developed with wide margins of safety.

answer.text: Drinking-water quality guidelines identify microbiological, physical, chemical and radiological parameters that have been found in drinking water. Health Canada has established more than 100 objectives for a host of contaminants in drinking water. Guidelines recommend measuring concentrations of chemical substances such as metals (e.g., lead, mercury) and other inorganic compounds, pesticides, radionuclides, and drinking water disinfection by-products (e.g., trihalomethanes) as well as microbial parameters such as bacteria, viruses and parasites in raw, treated and distributed drinking water. Densities of disease-causing organisms or concentrations of hazardous or toxic chemicals or radioactive substances should not exceed human health objectives, standards, or guidelines. Most contaminants in drinking water rarely exceed guidelines and many are below their analytical detection limit. Guidelines are based on lifetime exposures and have been developed with wide margins of safety.
